34|>>> c1 = Coordinates(1, 2) 35|>>> c1 36|Coordinates(x=1, y=2) 37|>>> c2 = Coordinates(x=2, y=1) 38|>>> c2 39|Coordinates(x=2, y=1) 40|>>> c1 == c2 41|False 42|``` 43| 44|As shown, the generated `__init__` method allows for both positional and keyword arguments. 45| 46|--- 47| 48|Unlike Data Classes, *attrs* doesn't force you to use type annotations. 49|So, the previous example could also have been written as: 50| 51|```{doctest} 52|>>> @define 53|... class Coordinates: 54|... x = field() 55|... y = field() 56|>>> Coordinates(1, 2) 57|Coordinates(x=1, y=2) 58|``` 59| 60|:::{caution} 61|If a class body contains a field that is defined using {func}`attrs.field` (or {func}`attr.ib`), but **lacks a type annotation**, *attrs* switches to a no-typing mode and ignores fields that have type annotations but are not defined using {func}`attrs.field` (or {func}`attr.ib`). 62|::: 63| 64|--- 65| 66|For private attributes, *attrs* will strip the leading underscores for keyword arguments: 67| 68|```{doctest} 69|>>> @define 70|... class C: 71|... _x: int 72|>>> C(x=1) 73|C(_x=1) 74|``` 75| 76|If you want to initialize your private attributes yourself, you can do that too: 77| 78|```{doctest} 79|>>> @define 80|... class C: 81|... _x: int = field(init=False, default=42) 82|>>> C() 83|C(_x=42) 84|>>> C(23) 85|Traceback (most recent call last): 86| ... 87|TypeError: __init__() takes exactly 1 argument (2 given) 88|``` 89| 90|If you prefer to expose your privates, you can use keyword argument aliases: 91| 92|```{doctest} 93|>>> @define 94|... class C: 95|... _x: int = field(alias="_x") 96|>>> C(_x=1) 97|C(_x=1) 98|``` 99| 100|An additional way of defining attributes is supported too. 101|This is useful in times when you want to enhance classes that are not yours (nice `__repr__` for Django models anyone?): 102| 103|```{doctest} 104|>>> class SomethingFromSomeoneElse: 105|... def __init__(self, x): 106|... self.x = x 107|>>> SomethingFromSomeoneElse = define( 108|... these={ 109|... "x": field() 110|... }, init=False)(SomethingFromSomeoneElse) 111|>>> SomethingFromSomeoneElse(1) 112|SomethingFromSomeoneElse(x=1) 113|``` 114| 115|[Subclassing is bad for you](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3MNVP9-hglc) (except when doing [strict specialization](https://hynek.me/articles/python-subclassing-redux/)), but *attrs* will still do what you'd hope for: 116| 117|```{doctest} 118|>>> @define(slots=False) 119|... class A: 120|... a: int 121|... def get_a(self): 122|... return self.a 123|>>> @define(slots=False) 124|... class B: 125|... b: int 126|>>> @define(slots=False) 127|... class C(B, A): 128|... c: int 129|>>> i = C(1, 2, 3) 130|>>> i 131|C(a=1, b=2, c=3) 132|>>> i == C(1, 2, 3) 133|True 134|>>> i.get_a() 135|1 136|``` 137| 138|{term}`Slotted classes `, which are the default for the new APIs, don't play well with multiple inheritance so we don't use them in the example. 139| 140|The order of the attributes is defined by the [MRO](https://www.python.org/download/releases/2.3/mro/). 141| 142| 143|### Keyword-only Attributes 144| 145|You can also add [keyword-only](https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#keyword-only-parameter) attributes: 146| 147|```{doctest} 148|>>> @define 149|... class A: 150|... a: int = field(kw_only=True) 151|>>> A() 152|Traceback (most recent call last): 153|... 154|TypeError: A() missing 1 required keyword-only argument: 'a' 155|>>> A(a=1) 156|A(a=1) 157|``` 158| 159|`kw_only` may also be specified at decorator level, and will apply to all attributes: 160| 161|```{doctest} 162|>>> @define(kw_only=True) 163|... class A: 164|... a: int 165|... b: int 166|>>> A(1, 2) 167|Traceback (most recent call last): 168|... 169|TypeError: __init__() takes 1 positional argument but 3 were given 170|>>> A(a=1, b=2) 171|A(a=1, b=2) 172|``` 173| 174|If you create an attribute with `init=False`, the `kw_only` argument is ignored. 175| 176|Keyword-only attributes allow subclasses to add attributes without default values, even if the base class defines attributes with default values: 177| 178|```{doctest} 179|>>> @define 180|... class A: 181|... a: int = 0 182|>>> @define 183|... class B(A): 184|... b: int = field(kw_only=True) 185|>>> B(b=1) 186|B(a=0, b=1) 187|>>> B() 188|Traceback (most recent call last): 189|... 190|TypeError: B() missing 1 required keyword-only argument: 'b' 191|``` 192| 193|If you don't set `kw_only=True`, then there is no valid attribute ordering, and you'll get an error: 194| 195|```{doctest} 196|>>> @define 197|... class A: 198|... a: int = 0 199|>>> @define 200|... class B(A): 201|... b: int 202|Traceback (most recent call last): 203|... 204|ValueError: No mandatory attributes allowed after an attribute with a default value or factory. Attribute in question: Attribute(name='b', default=NOTHING, validator=None, repr=True, cmp=True, hash=None, init=True, converter=None, metadata=mappingproxy({}), type=int, kw_only=False) 205|``` 206| 207|(asdict)= 208| 209|## Converting to Collections Types 210| 211|When you have a class with data, it often is very convenient to transform that class into a {class}`dict` (for example if you want to serialize it to JSON): 212| 213|```{doctest} 214|>>> from attrs import asdict 215|>>> asdict(Coordinates(x=1, y=2)) 216|{'x': 1, 'y': 2} 217|``` 218| 219|Some fields cannot or should not be transformed. 220|For that, {func}`attrs.asdict` offers a callback that decides whether an attribute should be included: 221| 222|```{doctest} 223|>>> @define 224|... class User: 225|... email: str 226|... password: str 227| 228|>>> @define 229|... class UserList: 230|... users: list[User] 231| 232|>>> asdict(UserList([User("jane@doe.invalid", "s33kred"), 233|... User("joe@doe.invalid", "p4ssw0rd")]), 234|... filter=lambda attr, value: attr.name != "password") 235|{'users': [{'email': 'jane@doe.invalid'}, {'email': 'joe@doe.invalid'}]} 236|``` 237| 238|For the common case where you want to [`include`](attrs.filters.include) or [`exclude`](attrs.filters.exclude) certain types, string name or attributes, *attrs* ships with a few helpers: 239| 240|```{doctest} 241|>>> from attrs import asdict, filters, fields 242| 243|>>> @define 244|... class User: 245|... login: str 246|... password: str 247|... email: str 248|... id: int 249| 250|>>> asdict( 251|... User("jane", "s33kred", "jane@example.com", 42), 252|... filter=filters.exclude(fields(User).password, "email", int)) 253|{'login': 'jane'} 254| 255|>>> @define 256|... class C: 257|... x: str 258|... y: str 259|... z: int 260| 261|>>> asdict(C("foo", "2", 3), 262|... filter=filters.include(int, fields(C).x)) 263|{'x': 'foo', 'z': 3} 264| 265|>>> asdict(C("foo", "2", 3), 266|... filter=filters.include(fields(C).x, "z")) 267|{'x': 'foo', 'z': 3} 268|``` 269| 270|:::{note} 271|Though using string names directly is convenient, mistyping attribute names will silently do the wrong thing and neither Python nor your type checker can help you. 272|{func}`attrs.fields()` will raise an `AttributeError` when the field doesn't exist while literal string names won't. 273|Using {func}`attrs.fields()` to get attributes is worth being recommended in most cases. 274| 275|```{doctest} 276|>>> asdict( 277|... User("jane", "s33kred", "jane@example.com", 42), 278|... filter=filters.exclude("passwd") 279|... ) 280|{'login': 'jane', 'password': 's33kred', 'email': 'jane@example.com', 'id': 42} 281| 282|>>> asdict( 283|... User("jane", "s33kred", "jane@example.com", 42), 284|... filter=fields(User).passwd 285|... ) 286|Traceback (most recent call last): 287|... 288|AttributeError: 'UserAttributes' object has no attribute 'passwd'. Did you mean: 'password'? 289|``` 290|::: 291| 292|Other times, all you want is a tuple and *attrs* won't let you down: 293| 294|```{doctest} 295|>>> import sqlite3 296|>>> from attrs import astuple 297| 298|>>> @define 299|... class Foo: 300|... a: int 301|... b: int 302| 303|>>> foo = Foo(2, 3) 304|>>> with sqlite3.connect(":memory:") as conn: 305|... c = conn.cursor() 306|... c.execute("CREATE TABLE foo (x INTEGER PRIMARY KEY ASC, y)") #doctest: +ELLIPSIS 307|... c.execute("INSERT INTO foo VALUES (?, ?)", astuple(foo)) #doctest: +ELLIPSIS 308|... foo2 = Foo(*c.execute("SELECT x, y FROM foo").fetchone()) 309| 310| 311|>>> foo == foo2 312|True 313|``` 314| 315|For more advanced transformations and conversions, we recommend you look at a companion library (such as [*cattrs*](https://catt.rs/)). 316| 317| 318|## Defaults 319| 320|Sometimes you want to have default values for your initializer. 321|And sometimes you even want mutable objects as default values (ever accidentally used `def f(arg=[])`?). 322|*attrs* has you covered in both cases: 323| 324|```{doctest} 325|>>> import collections 326| 327|>>> @define 328|... class Connection: 329|... socket: int 330|... @classmethod 331|... def connect(cls, db_string): 332|... # ... connect somehow to db_string ... 333|... return cls(socket=42) 334| 335|>>> @define 336|... class ConnectionPool: 337|... db_string: str 338|... pool: collections.deque = Factory(collections.deque) 339|... debug: bool = False 340|... def get_connection(self): 341|... try: 342|... return self.pool.pop() 343|... except IndexError: 344|... if self.debug: 345|... print("New connection!") 346|... return Connection.connect(self.db_string) 347|... def free_connection(self, conn): 348|... if self.debug: 349|... print("Connection returned!") 350|... self.pool.appendleft(conn) 351|... 352|>>> cp = ConnectionPool("postgres://localhost") 353|>>> cp 354|ConnectionPool(db_string='postgres://localhost', pool=deque([]), debug=False) 355|>>> conn = cp.get_connection() 356|>>> conn 357|Connection(socket=42) 358|>>> cp.free_connection(conn) 359|>>> cp 360|ConnectionPool(db_string='postgres://localhost', pool=deque([Connection(socket=42)]), debug=False) 361|``` 362| 363|More information on why class methods for constructing objects are awesome can be found in this insightful [blog post](https://web.archive.org/web/20210130220433/http://as.ynchrono.us/2014/12/asynchronous-object-initialization.html). 364| 365|Default factories can also be set using the `factory` argument to {func}`~attrs.field`, and using a decorator. 366|The method receives the partially initialized instance which enables you to base a default value on other attributes: 367| 368|```{doctest} 369|>>> @define 370|... class C: 371|... x: int = 1 372|... y: int = field() 373|... @y.default 374|... def _any_name_except_a_name_of_an_attribute(self): 375|... return self.x + 1 376|... z: list = field(factory=list) 377|>>> C() 378|C(x=1, y=2, z=[]) 379|``` 380| 381|Please keep in mind that the decorator approach *only* works if the attribute in question has a {func}`~attrs.field` assigned to it. 382|As a result, annotating an attribute with a type is *not* enough if you use `@default`. 383| 384|(examples-validators)= 385| 386|## Validators 387| 388|Although your initializers should do as little as possible (ideally: just initialize your instance according to the arguments!), it can come in handy to do some kind of validation on the arguments. 389| 390|*attrs* offers two ways to define validators for each attribute and it's up to you to choose which one suits your style and project better. 391| 392|You can use a decorator: 393| 394|```{doctest} 395|>>> @define 396|... class C: 397|... x: int = field() 398|... @x.validator 399|... def check(self, attribute, value): 400|... if value > 42: 401|... raise ValueError("x must be smaller or equal to 42") 402|>>> C(42) 403|C(x=42) 404|>>> C(43) 405|Traceback (most recent call last): 406| ... 407|ValueError: x must be smaller or equal to 42 408|``` 409| 410|...or a callable... 411| 412|```{doctest} 413|>>> from attrs import validators 414| 415|>>> def x_smaller_than_y(instance, attribute, value): 416|... if value >= instance.y: 417|... raise ValueError("'x' has to be smaller than 'y'!") 418|>>> @define 419|... class C: 420|... x: int = field(validator=[validators.instance_of(int), 421|... x_smaller_than_y]) 422|... y: int 423|>>> C(x=3, y=4) 424|C(x=3, y=4) 425|>>> C(x=4, y=3) 426|Traceback (most recent call last): 427| ... 428|ValueError: 'x' has to be smaller than 'y'! 429|``` 430| 431|...or both at once: 432| 433|```{doctest} 434|>>> @define 435|... class C: 436|... x: int = field(validator=validators.instance_of(int)) 437|... @x.validator 438|... def fits_byte(self, attribute, value): 439|... if not 0 <= value < 256: 440|... raise ValueError("value out of bounds") 441|>>> C(128) 442|C(x=128) 443|>>> C("128") 444|Traceback (most recent call last): 445| ... 446|TypeError: ("'x' must be (got '128' that is a ).", Attribute(name='x', default=NOTHING, validator=[>, ], repr=True, cmp=True, hash=True, init=True, metadata=mappingproxy({}), type=int, converter=None, kw_only=False), , '128') 447|>>> C(256) 448|Traceback (most recent call last): 449| ... 450|ValueError: value out of bounds 451|``` 452| 453|Please note that the decorator approach only works if -- and only if! -- the attribute in question has a {func}`~attrs.field` assigned. 454|Therefore if you use `@validator`, it is *not* enough to annotate said attribute with a type. 455| 456|*attrs* ships with a bunch of validators, make sure to [check them out](api-validators) before writing your own: 457| 458|```{doctest} 459|>>> @define 460|... class C: 461|... x: int = field(validator=validators.instance_of(int)) 462|>>> C(42) 463|C(x=42) 464|>>> C("42") 465|Traceback (most recent call last): 466| ... 467|TypeError: ("'x' must be (got '42' that is a ).", Attribute(name='x', default=NOTHING, factory=NOTHING, validator=>, type=None, kw_only=False), , '42') 468|``` 469| 470|If using the old-school {func}`attr.s` decorator, validators only run on initialization by default. 471|If using the newer {func}`attrs.define` and friends, validators run on initialization *and* on attribute setting. 472|This behavior can be changed using the *on_setattr* argument. 473| 474|Check out {ref}`validators` for more details. 475| 476| 477|## Conversion 478| 479|Attributes can have a `converter` function specified, which will be called with the attribute's passed-in value to get a new value to use. 480|This can be useful for doing type-conversions on values that you don't want to force your callers to do. 481| 482|```{doctest} 483|>>> @define 484|... class C: 485|... x: int = field(converter=int) 486|>>> o = C("1") 487|>>> o.x 488|1 489|>>> o.x = "2" 490|>>> o.x 491|2 492|``` 493| 494|If using the old-school {func}`attr.s` decorator, converters only run on initialization by default. 495|If using the newer {func}`attrs.define` and friends, converters run on initialization *and* on attribute setting. 496|This behavior can be changed using the *on_setattr* argument. 497| 498|Check out {ref}`converters` for more details. 499| 500| 501|## Running Custom Code Before/After Setting Attributes 502| 503|If your `__setattr__` hook needs to run custom code before **and** after setting attributes, you can pass a generator to the `on_setattr` argument: 504| 505|```{doctest} 506|>>> from typing import Generator 507|>>> def gen_hook(instance: Any, attribute: attr.Attribute[int], value: Any) -> Generator[int]: 508|... print(f"value coming in: {value!r}") 509|... new_value = int(value) * 2 + 286 510|... yield new_value 511|... print(f"set {attribute.name} to {new_value!r}") 512|>>> @define 513|... class C: 514|... x: int = field(on_setattr=gen_hook) 515|>>> c = C(42) # doesn't run on __init__ 516|>>> c.x = "67" 517|value coming in: '67' 518|set x to 420 519|>>> c.x 520|420 521|``` 522| 523| 524|(metadata)= 525| 526|## Metadata 527| 528|All *attrs* attributes may include arbitrary metadata in the form of a read-only dictionary. 529| 530|```{doctest} 531|>>> from attrs import fields 532| 533|>>> @define 534|... class C: 535|... x = field(metadata={'my_metadata': 1}) 536|>>> fields(C).x.metadata 537|mappingproxy({'my_metadata': 1}) 538|>>> fields(C).x.metadata['my_metadata'] 539|1 540|``` 541| 542|Metadata is not used by *attrs*, and is meant to enable rich functionality in third-party libraries. 543|The metadata dictionary follows the normal dictionary rules: 544|Keys need to be hashable, and both keys and values are recommended to be immutable. 545| 546|If you're the author of a third-party library with *attrs* integration, please see [*Extending Metadata*](extending-metadata). 547| 548| 549|## Types 550| 551|*attrs* also allows you to associate a type with an attribute using either the *type* argument to using {pep}`526`-annotations or {func}`attrs.field`/{func}`attr.ib`: 552| 553|```{doctest} 554|>>> @define 555|... class C: 556|... x: int 557|>>> fields(C).x.type 558| 559| 560|>>> import attr 561|>>> @attr.s 562|... class C: 563|... x = attr.ib(type=int) 564|>>> fields(C).x.type 565| 566|``` 567| 568|If you don't mind annotating *all* attributes, you can even drop the `attrs.field` and assign default values instead: 569| 570|```{doctest} 571|>>> import typing 572| 573|>>> @define 574|... class AutoC: 575|... cls_var: typing.ClassVar[int] = 5 # this one is ignored 576|... l: list[int] = Factory(list) 577|... x: int = 1 578|... foo: str = "every attrib needs a type if auto_attribs=True" 579|... bar: typing.Any = None 580|>>> fields(AutoC).l.type 581|list[int] 582|>>> fields(AutoC).x.type 583| 584|>>> fields(AutoC).foo.type 585| 586|>>> fields(AutoC).bar.type 587|typing.Any 588|>>> AutoC() 589|AutoC(l=[], x=1, foo='every attrib needs a type if auto_attribs=True', bar=None) 590|>>> AutoC.cls_var 591|5 592|``` 593| 594|The generated `__init__` method will have an attribute called `__annotations__` that contains this type information. 595| 596|If your annotations contain strings (for example, forward references), 597|you can resolve these after all references have been defined by using {func}`attrs.resolve_types`. 598|This will replace the *type* attribute in the respective fields. 599| 600|```{doctest} 601|>>> from attrs import resolve_types 602| 603|>>> @define 604|... class A: 605|... a: 'list[A]' 606|... b: 'B' 607|... 608|>>> @define 609|... class B: 610|... a: A 611|... 612|>>> fields(A).a.type 613|'list[A]' 614|>>> fields(A).b.type 615|'B' 616|>>> resolve_types(A, globals(), locals()) 617| 618|>>> fields(A).a.type 619|list[A] 620|>>> fields(A).b.type 621| 622|``` 623| 624|:::{note} 625|If you find yourself using string type annotations to handle forward references, wrap the entire type annotation in quotes instead of only the type you need a forward reference to (so `'list[A]'` instead of `list['A']`). 626|This is a limitation of the Python typing system. 627|::: 628| 629|:::{warning} 630|*attrs* itself doesn't have any features that work on top of type metadata. 631|However it's useful for writing your own validators or serialization frameworks. 632|::: 633| 634| 635|## Slots 636| 637|{term}`Slotted classes ` have several advantages on CPython. 638|Defining `__slots__` by hand is tedious, in *attrs* it's just a matter of using {func}`attrs.define` or passing `slots=True` to {func}`attr.s`: 639| 640|```{doctest} 641|>>> @define 642|... class Coordinates: 643|... x: int 644|... y: int 645| 646|>>> import attr 647| 648|>>> @attr.s(slots=True) 649|... class Coordinates: 650|... x: int 651|... y: int 652|``` 653| 654|{func}`~attrs.define` sets `slots=True` by default. 655| 656| 657|## Immutability 658| 659|Sometimes you have instances that shouldn't be changed after instantiation. 660|Immutability is especially popular in functional programming and is generally a very good thing. 661|If you'd like to enforce it, *attrs* will try to help: 662| 663|```{doctest} 664|>>> from attrs import frozen 665| 666|>>> @frozen 667|... class C: 668|... x: int 669|>>> i = C(1) 670|>>> i.x = 2 671|Traceback (most recent call last): 672| ... 673|attrs.exceptions.FrozenInstanceError: can't set attribute 674|>>> i.x 675|1 676|``` 677| 678|Please note that true immutability is impossible in Python but it will [get](how-frozen) you 99% there. 679|By themselves, immutable classes are useful for long-lived objects that should never change; like configurations for example. 680| 681|In order to use them in regular program flow, you'll need a way to easily create new instances with changed attributes. 682|In Clojure that function is called [*assoc*](https://clojuredocs.org/clojure.core/assoc) and *attrs* shamelessly imitates it: {func}`attrs.evolve`: 683| 684|```{doctest} 685|>>> from attrs import evolve, frozen 686| 687|>>> @frozen 688|... class C: 689|... x: int 690|... y: int 691|>>> i1 = C(1, 2) 692|>>> i1 693|C(x=1, y=2) 694|>>> i2 = evolve(i1, y=3) 695|>>> i2 696|C(x=1, y=3) 697|>>> i1 == i2 698|False 699|``` 700| 701|On Python 3.13 and later, you can also use {func}`copy.replace` from the standard library: 702| 703|```{doctest} 704|>>> import copy 705|>>> @frozen 706|... class C: 707|... x: int 708|... y: int 709|>>> i = C(1, 2) 710|>>> copy.replace(i, y=3) 711|C(x=1, y=3) 712|``` 713| 714| 715|## Other Goodies 716| 717|When building systems that have something resembling a plugin interface, you may want to have a registry of all classes that implement a certain interface: 718| 719|```{doctest} 720|>>> REGISTRY = [] 721|>>> class Base: # does NOT have to be an attrs class! 722|... @classmethod 723|... def __attrs_init_subclass__(cls): 724|... REGISTRY.append(cls) 725|>>> @define 726|... class Impl(Base): 727|... pass 728|>>> REGISTRY 729|[] 730|``` 731| 732|Sometimes you may want to create a class programmatically. 733|*attrs* gives you {func}`attrs.make_class` for that: 734| 735|```{doctest} 736|>>> from attrs import make_class 737|>>> @define 738|... class C1: 739|... x = field(type=int) 740|... y = field() 741|>>> C2 = make_class("C2", {"x": field(type=int), "y": field()}) 742|>>> fields(C1) == fields(C2) 743|True 744|>>> fields(C2).x.type 745| 746|``` 747| 748|You can still have power over the attributes if you pass a dictionary of name: {func}`~attrs.field` mappings and can pass the same arguments as you can to `@attrs.define`: 749| 750|```{doctest} 751|>>> C = make_class("C", {"x": field(default=42), 752|... "y": field(default=Factory(list))}, 753|... repr=False) 754|>>> i = C() 755|>>> i # no repr added! 756|<__main__.C object at ...> 757|>>> i.x 758|42 759|>>> i.y 760|[] 761|``` 762| 763|If you need to dynamically make a class with {func}`~attrs.make_class` and it needs to be a subclass of something else than {class}`object`, use the `bases` argument: 764| 765|```{doctest} 766|>>> class D: 767|... def __eq__(self, other): 768|... return True # arbitrary example 769|>>> C = make_class("C", {}, bases=(D,), cmp=False) 770|>>> isinstance(C(), D) 771|True 772|``` 773| 774|Sometimes, you want to have your class's `__init__` method do more than just 775|the initialization, validation, etc. that gets done for you automatically when 776|using `@define`. 777|To do this, just define a `__attrs_post_init__` method in your class. 778|It will get called at the end of the generated `__init__` method. 779| 780|```{doctest} 781|>>> @define 782|... class C: 783|... x: int 784|... y: int 785|... z: int = field(init=False) 786|... 787|... def __attrs_post_init__(self): 788|... self.z = self.x + self.y 789|>>> obj = C(x=1, y=2) 790|>>> obj 791|C(x=1, y=2, z=3) 792|``` 793| 794|You can exclude single attributes from certain methods: 795| 796|```{doctest} 797|>>> @define 798|... class C: 799|... user: str 800|... password: str = field(repr=False) 801|>>> C("me", "s3kr3t") 802|C(user='me') 803|``` 804| 805|Alternatively, to influence how the generated `__repr__()` method formats a specific attribute, specify a custom callable to be used instead of the `repr()` built-in initialization happens in the `__init__` method. 4|Generally speaking, you should keep as little logic as possible in it, and you should think about what the class needs and not how it is going to be instantiated. 5| 6|Passing complex objects into `__init__` and then using them to derive data for the class unnecessarily couples your new class with the old class which makes it harder to test and also will cause problems later. 7| 8|So assuming you use an ORM and want to extract 2D points from a row object, do not write code like this: 9| 10|```python 11|class Point: 12| def __init__(self, database_row): 13| self.x = database_row.x 14| self.y = database_row.y 15| 16| 17|pt = Point(row) 18|``` 19| 20|Instead, write a {obj}`classmethod` that will extract it for you: 21| 22|```python 23|@define 24|class Point: 25| x: float 26| y: float 27| 28| @classmethod 29| def from_row(cls, row): 30| return cls(row.x, row.y) 31| 32| 33|pt = Point.from_row(row) 34|``` 35| 36|This is sometimes called a *named constructor* or a *factory method*. 37| 38|Now, you can instantiate `Point`s without creating fake row objects in your tests. 39|You can also have as many smart creation helpers as you want. 40|This flexibility is useful because additional data sources tend to appear over time. 41| 42|--- 43| 44|For similar reasons, we strongly discourage from patterns like: 45| 46|```python 47|pt = Point(**row.attributes) 48|``` 49| 50|which couples your classes to the database data model. 51|Try to design your classes in a way that is clean and convenient to use -- not based on your database format. 52|The database format can change anytime and you're stuck with a bad class design that is hard to change. 53|Embrace functions and classmethods as a filter between reality and what's best for you to work with. 54| 55|:::{important} 56|While *attrs*'s initialization concepts (including the following sections about validators and converters) are powerful, they are **not** intended to replace a fully-featured serialization or validation system. 57| 58|We want to help you to write a `__init__` that you'd write by hand, but with less boilerplate. 59| 60|If you look for powerful-yet-unintrusive serialization and validation for your *attrs* classes, have a look at our sibling project [*cattrs*](https://catt.rs/) or our [third-party extensions](https://github.com/python-attrs/attrs/wiki/Extensions-to-attrs). 61| 62|This separation of creating classes and serializing them is a conscious design decision. 63|We don't think that your business model and your serialization format should be coupled. 64|::: 65| 66|(private-attributes)= 67| 68|## Private Attributes and Aliases 69| 70|One thing people tend to find confusing is the treatment of private attributes that start with an underscore. 71|Although there is [a convention](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/classes.html#tut-private) that members of an object that start with an underscore should be treated as private, consider that a core feature of *attrs* is to automatically create an `__init__` method whose arguments correspond to the members. 72|There is no corresponding convention for private arguments: the entire signature of a function is its public interface to be used by callers. 73| 74|However, it is sometimes useful to accept a public argument when an object is constructed, but treat that attribute as private after the object is created, perhaps to maintain some invariant. 75|As a convenience for this use case, the default behavior of *attrs* is that if you specify a member that starts with an underscore, it will strip the underscore from the name when it creates the `__init__` method signature: 76| 77|```{doctest} 78|>>> import inspect 79|>>> from attrs import define 80|>>> @define 81|... class FileDescriptor: 82|... _fd: int 83|>>> inspect.signature(FileDescriptor.__init__) 84| None> 85|``` 86| 87|Even if you're not using this feature, it's important to be aware of it because it can lead to surprising syntax errors: 88| 89|```{doctest} 90|>>> @define 91|... class C: 92|... _1: int 93|Traceback (most recent call last): 94| ... 95|SyntaxError: invalid syntax 96|``` 97| 98|In this case a valid attribute name `_1` got transformed into an invalid argument name `1`. 99| 100|Whether this feature is useful to you is a matter of taste. 101|If your taste differs, you can use the *alias* argument to {func}`attrs.field` to explicitly set the argument name. 102|This can be used to override private attribute handling, or make other arbitrary changes to `__init__` argument names. 103| 104|```{doctest} 105|>>> from attrs import field 106|>>> @define 107|... class C: 108|... _x: int = field(alias="_x") 109|... y: int = field(alias="distasteful_y") 110|... _1: int = field(alias="underscore1") 111|>>> inspect.signature(C.__init__) 112| None> 113|``` 114| 115|(defaults)= 116| 117|## Defaults 118| 119|Sometimes you don't want to pass all attribute values to a class. 120|And sometimes, certain attributes aren't even intended to be passed but you want to allow for customization anyways for easier testing. 121| 122|This is when default values come into play: 123| 124|```{doctest} 125|>>> from attrs import Factory 126|>>> @define 127|... class C: 128|... a: int = 42 129|... b: list = field(factory=list) 130|... c: list = Factory(list) # syntactic sugar for above 131|... d: dict = field() 132|... @d.default 133|... def _any_name_except_a_name_of_an_attribute(self): 134|... return {} 135|>>> C() 136|C(a=42, b=[], c=[], d={}) 137|``` 138| 139|It's important that the decorated method -- or any other method or property! -- doesn't have the same name as the attribute, otherwise it would overwrite the attribute definition. 140| 141|Similar to the [common gotcha with mutable default arguments](https://docs.python-guide.org/writing/gotchas/#mutable-default-arguments), `default=[]` will *not* do what you may think it might do: 142| 143|```{doctest} 144|>>> @define 145|... class C: 146|... x = [] 147|>>> i = C() 148|>>> k = C() 149|>>> i.x.append(42) 150|>>> k.x 151|[42] 152|``` 153| 154|This is why *attrs* comes with factory options. 155| 156|:::{warning} 157|Please note that the decorator based defaults have one gotcha: 158|they are executed when the attribute is set, that means depending on the order of attributes, the `self` object may not be fully initialized when they're called. 159| 160|Therefore you should use `self` as little as possible. 161| 162|Even the smartest of us can [get confused](https://github.com/python-attrs/attrs/issues/289) by what happens if you pass partially initialized objects around. 163|::: 164| 165|(validators)= 166| 167|## Validators 168| 169|Another thing that definitely *does* belong in `__init__` is checking the resulting instance for invariants. 170|This is why *attrs* has the concept of validators. 171| 172| 173|### Decorator 174| 175|The most straightforward way is using the attribute's `validator` method as a decorator. 176| 177|The method has to accept three arguments: 178| 179|1. the *instance* that's being validated (aka `self`), 180|2. the *attribute* that it's validating, and finally 181|3. the *value* that is passed for it. 182| 183|These values are passed as *positional arguments*, therefore their names don't matter. 184| 185|If the value does not pass the validator's standards, it just raises an appropriate exception. 186| 187|```{doctest} 188|>>> @define 189|... class C: 190|... x: int = field() 191|... @x.validator 192|... def _check_x(self, attribute, value): 193|... if value > 42: 194|... raise ValueError("x must be smaller or equal to 42") 195|>>> C(42) 196|C(x=42) 197|>>> C(43) 198|Traceback (most recent call last): 199| ... 200|ValueError: x must be smaller or equal to 42 201|``` 202| 203|Again, it's important that the decorated method doesn't have the same name as the attribute and that the {func}`attrs.field` helper is used. 204| 205| 206|### Callables 207| 208|If you want to reuse your validators, you should have a look at the `validator` argument to {func}`attrs.field`. 209| 210|It takes either a callable or a list of callables (usually functions) and treats them as validators that receive the same arguments as with the decorator approach. 211|Also as with the decorator approach, they are passed as *positional arguments* so you can name them however you want. 212| 213|Since the validators run *after* the instance is initialized, you can refer to other attributes while validating: 214| 215|```{doctest} 216|>>> import attrs 217|>>> def x_smaller_than_y(instance, attribute, value): 218|... if value >= instance.y: 219|... raise ValueError("'x' has to be smaller than 'y'!") 220|>>> @define 221|... class C: 222|... x = field(validator=[attrs.validators.instance_of(int), 223|... x_smaller_than_y]) 224|... y = field() 225|>>> C(x=3, y=4) 226|C(x=3, y=4) 227|>>> C(x=4, y=3) 228|Traceback (most recent call last): 229| ... 230|ValueError: 'x' has to be smaller than 'y'! 231|``` 232| 233|This example demonstrates a convenience shortcut: 234|Passing a list of validators directly is equivalent to passing them wrapped in the {obj}`attrs.validators.and_` validator and all validators must pass. 235| 236|*attrs* won't intercept your changes to those attributes but you can always call {func}`attrs.validate` on any instance to verify that it's still valid: 237| 238|When using {func}`attrs.define` or [`attrs.frozen`](attrs.frozen), however, *attrs* will run the validators even when setting the attribute. 239| 240|```{doctest} 241|>>> i = C(4, 5) 242|>>> i.x = 5 243|Traceback (most recent call last): 244| ... 245|ValueError: 'x' has to be smaller than 'y'! 246|``` 247| 248|*attrs* ships with a bunch of validators, make sure to [check them out]( api-validators) before writing your own: 249| 250|```{doctest} 251|>>> @define 252|... class C: 253|... x = field(validator=attrs.validators.instance_of(int)) 254|>>> C(42) 255|C(x=42) 256|>>> C("42") 257|Traceback (most recent call last): 258| ... 259|TypeError: ("'x' must be (got '42' that is a ).", Attribute(name='x', default=NOTHING, factory=NOTHING, validator=>, type=None), , '42') 260|``` 261| 262|Of course you can mix and match the two approaches at your convenience. 263|If you use both ways to define validators for an attribute, they are both ran: 264| 265|```{doctest} 266|>>> @define 267|... class C: 268|... x = field(validator=attrs.validators.instance_of(int)) 269|... @x.validator 270|... def fits_byte(self, attribute, value): 271|... if not 0 <= value < 256: 272|... raise ValueError("value out of bounds") 273|>>> C(128) 274|C(x=128) 275|>>> C("128") 276|Traceback (most recent call last): 277| ... 278|TypeError: ("'x' must be (got '128' that is a ).", Attribute(name='x', default=NOTHING, validator=[>, ], repr=True, cmp=True, hash=True, init=True, metadata=mappingproxy({}), type=None, converter=None), , '128') 279|>>> C(256) 280|Traceback (most recent call last): 281| ... 282|ValueError: value out of bounds 283|``` 284| 285|Finally, validators can be globally disabled: 286| 287|```{doctest} 288|>>> attrs.validators.set_disabled(True) 289|>>> C("128") 290|C(x='128') 291|>>> attrs.validators.set_disabled(False) 292|>>> C("128") 293|Traceback (most recent call last): 294| ... 295|TypeError: ("'x' must be (got '128' that is a ).", Attribute(name='x', default=NOTHING, validator=[>, ], repr=True, cmp=True, hash=True, init=True, metadata=mappingproxy({}), type=None, converter=None), , '128') 296|``` 297| 298|... or within a context manager: 299| 300|```{doctest} 301|>>> with attrs.validators.disabled(): 302|... C("128") 303|C(x='128') 304|>>> C("128") 305|Traceback (most recent call last): 306| ... 307|TypeError: ("'x' must be (got '128' that is a ).", Attribute(name='x', default=NOTHING, validator=[>, ], repr=True, cmp=True, hash=True, init=True, metadata=mappingproxy({}), type=None, converter=None), , '128') 308|``` 309| 310|(converters)= 311| 312|## Converters 313| 314|Sometimes, it is necessary to normalize the values coming in, therefore *attrs* comes with converters. 315| 316|Attributes can have a `converter` function specified, which will be called with the attribute's passed-in value to get a new value to use. 317|This can be useful for doing type-conversions on values that you don't want to force your callers to do. 318| 319|```{doctest} 320|>>> @define 321|... class C: 322|... x = field(converter=int) 323|>>> o = C("1") 324|>>> o.x 325|1 326|>>> o.x = "2" 327|>>> o.x 328|2 329|``` 330| 331|Converters are run *before* validators, so you can use validators to check the final form of the value. 332| 333|```{doctest} 334|>>> def validate_x(instance, attribute, value): 335|... if value < 0: 336|... raise ValueError("x must be at least 0.") 337|>>> @define 338|... class C: 339|... x = field(converter=int, validator=validate_x) 340|>>> o = C("0") 341|>>> o.x 342|0 343|>>> C("-1") 344|Traceback (most recent call last): 345| ... 346|ValueError: x must be at least 0. 347|``` 348| 349|Arguably, you can abuse converters as one-argument validators: 350| 351|```{doctest} 352|>>> C("x") 353|Traceback (most recent call last): 354| ... 355|ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'x' 356|``` 357| 358|If a converter's first argument has a type annotation, that type will appear in the signature for `__init__`. 359|A converter will override an explicit type annotation or `type` argument. 360| 361|```{doctest} 362|>>> def str2int(x: str) -> int: 363|... return int(x) 364|>>> @define 365|... class C: 366|... x = field(converter=str2int) 367|>>> C.__init__.__annotations__ 368|{'return': None, 'x': } 369|``` 370| 371|If you need more control over the conversion process, you can wrap the converter with a {class}`attrs.Converter` and ask for the instance and/or the field that are being initialized: 372| 373|```{doctest} 374|>>> def complicated(value, self_, field): 375|... return int(value) * self_.factor + field.metadata["offset"] 376|>>> @define 377|... class C: 378|... factor = 5 # not an *attrs* field 379|... x = field( 380|... metadata={"offset": 200}, 381|... converter=attrs.Converter( 382|... complicated, 383|... takes_self=True, takes_field=True 384|... )) 385|>>> C("42") 386|C(x=410) 387|``` 388| 389|Or as a decorator 390| 391|```{doctest} 392|>>> from typing import ClassVar 393|>>> @define 394|... class C: 395|... factor: ClassVar[int] = 5 # ClassVars are ignored by attrs 396|... x: int = field(metadata={"offset": 200}) 397|... @x.converter 398|... def _convert_x(self, attribute, value): 399|... return int(value) * self.factor + attribute.metadata["offset"] 400|>>> C("42") 401|C(x=410) 402|``` 403| 404| 405|## Hooking Yourself Into Initialization 406| 407|Generally speaking, the moment you realize the need of finer control – than what *attrs* offers – over how a class is instantiated, it's usually best to use a {obj}`classmethod` factory or to apply the [builder pattern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Builder_pattern). 408| 409|However, sometimes you need to do that one quick thing before or after your class is initialized. 410|For that purpose, *attrs* offers the following options: 411| 412|- `__attrs_pre_init__` is automatically detected and run *before* *attrs* starts initializing. 413| If `__attrs_pre_init__` takes more than the `self` argument, the *attrs*-generated `__init__` will call it with the same arguments it received itself. 414| This is useful if you need to inject a call to `super().__init__()` -- with or without arguments. 415| 416|- `__attrs_post_init__` is automatically detected and run *after* *attrs* is done initializing your instance. 417| This is useful if you want to derive some attribute from others or perform some kind of validation over the whole instance. 418| 419|- `__attrs_init__` is written and attached to your class *instead* of `__init__`, if *attrs* is told to not write one (when `init=False` or a by a combination of `auto_detect=True` and a custom `__init__`). 420| This is useful if you want full control over the initialization process, but don't want to set the attributes by hand. 421| 422| 423|### Pre Init 424| 425|The sole reason for the existence of `__attrs_pre_init__` is to give users the chance to call `super().__init__()`, because some subclassing-based APIs require that. 426| 427|```{doctest} 428|>>> @define 429|... class C: 430|... x: int 431|... def __attrs_pre_init__(self): 432|... super().__init__() 433|>>> C(42) 434|C(x=42) 435|``` 436| 437|If you need more control, use the custom init approach described next. 438| 439|:::{warning} 440|You never need to use `super()` with *attrs* classes that inherit from other *attrs* classes. 441|Each *attrs* class implements an `__init__` based on its own fields and those of all its base classes. 442| 443|You only need this escape hatch when subclassing non-*attrs* classes. 444|::: 445| 446| 447|### Custom Init 448| 449|If you tell *attrs* to not write an `__init__`, it will write an `__attrs_init__` instead, with the same code that it would have used for `__init__`. 450|You have full control over the initialization, but also have to type out the types of your arguments etc. 451|Here's an example of a manual default value: 452| 453|```{doctest} 454|>>> @define 455|... class C: 456|... x: int 457|... 458|... def __init__(self, x: int = 42): 459|... self.__attrs_init__(x) 460|>>> C() 461|C(x=42) 462|``` 463| 464| 465|### Post Init 466| 467|```{doctest} 468|>>> @define 469|... class C: 470|... x: int 471|... y: int = field(init=False) 472|... def __attrs_post_init__(self): 473|... self.y = self.x + 1 474|>>> C(1) 475|C(x=1, y=2) 476|``` 477| 478|Please note that you can't directly set attributes on frozen classes: 479| 480|```{doctest} 481|>>> @frozen 482|... class FrozenBroken: 483|... x: int 484|... y: int = field(init=False) 485|... def __attrs_post_init__(self): 486|... self.y = self.x + 1 487|>>> FrozenBroken(1) 488|Traceback (most recent call last): 489| ... 490|attrs.exceptions.FrozenInstanceError: can't set attribute 491|``` 492| 493|If you need to set attributes on a frozen class, you'll have to resort to the [same trick](how-frozen) as *attrs* and use {meth}`object.__setattr__`: 494| 495|```{doctest} 496|>>> @frozen 497|... class Frozen: 498|... x: int 499|... y: int = field(init=False) 500|... def __attrs_post_init__(self): 501|... object.__setattr__(self, "y", self.x + 1) 502|>>> Frozen(1) 503|Frozen(x=1, y=2) 504|``` 505| 506|Note that you *must not* access the hash code of the object in `__attrs_post_init__` if `cache_hash=True`. 507| 508| 509|## Order of Execution 510| 511|If present, the hooks are executed in the following order: 512| 513|1. `__attrs_pre_init__` (if present on *current* class) 514| 515|2. For each attribute, in the order it was declared: 516| 517| 1. default factory 518| 2. converter 519| 520|3. *all* validators 521| 522|4. `__attrs_post_init__` (if present on *current* class) 523| 524|Notably this means, that you can access all attributes from within your validators, but your converters have to deal with invalid values and have to return a valid value. 525| 526| 527|## Derived Attributes 528| 529|One of the most common *attrs* questions on *Stack Overflow* is how to have attributes that depend on other attributes. 530|For example if you have an API token and want to instantiate a web client that uses it for authentication. 531|Based on the previous sections, there are two approaches. 532| 533|The simpler one is using `__attrs_post_init__`: 534| 535|```python 536|@define 537|class APIClient: 538| token: str 539| client: WebClient = field(init=False) 540| 541| def __attrs_post_init__(self): 542| self.client = WebClient(self.token) 543|``` 544| 545|The second one is using a decorator-based default: 546| 547|```python 548|@define 549|class APIClient: 550| token: str 551| client: WebClient = field() # needed! attr.ib works too 552| 553| @client.default 554| def _client_factory(self): 555| return WebClient(self.token) 556|``` 557| 558|That said, and as pointed out in the beginning of the chapter, a better approach would be to have a factory class method: 559| 560|```python 561|@define 562|class APIClient: 563| client: WebClient 564| 565| @classmethod 566| def from_token(cls, token: str) -> "APIClient": 567| return cls(client=WebClient(token)) 568|``` 569| 570|This makes the class more testable. 571| 572|(init-subclass)= 573| 574|## *attrs* and `__init_subclass__` 575| 576|{meth}`object.__init_subclass__` is a special method that is called when a subclass of the class that defined it is created. 577| 578|For example: 579| 580|```{doctest} 581|>>> class Base: 582|... @classmethod 583|... def __init_subclass__(cls): 584|... print(f"Base has been subclassed by {cls}.") 585|>>> class Derived(Base): 586|... pass 587|Base has been subclassed by . 588|``` 589| 590|Unfortunately, a class decorator-based approach like *attrs* (or `dataclasses`) doesn't play well with `__init_subclass__`. 591|With {term}`dict classes`, it is run *before* the class has been processed by *attrs* and in the case of {term}`slotted classes`, where *attrs* has to *replace* the original class, `__init_subclass__` is called *twice*: once for the original class and once for the *attrs* class. 592| 593|To alleviate this, *attrs* provides `__attrs_init_subclass__` which is also called once the class is done assembling. 594|The base class doesn't even have to be an *attrs* class: 595| 596|```{doctest} 597|>>> class Base: 598|... @classmethod 599|... def __attrs_init_subclass__(cls): 600|... print(f"Base has been subclassed by attrs {cls}.") 601|>>> @define 602|... class Derived(Base): 603|... pass 604|Base has been subclassed by attrs . 605|``` --- END FILE: docs/init.md --- --- FILE: src/attrs/converters.py --- 1|# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT 2| 3|from attr.converters import * # noqa: F403 Everyone Needs*](https://glyph.twistedmatrix.com/2016/08/attrs.html). 4|It predates type annotations and hence Data Classes, but it masterfully illustrates the appeal of class-building packages. 5| 6| 7|## … Data Classes? 8| 9|{pep}`557` added Data Classes to [Python 3.7](https://docs.python.org/3.7/whatsnew/3.7.html#dataclasses). 10|They resemble *attrs* in many ways. 11| 12|They are the result of the Python community's [wish](https://mail.python.org/pipermail/python-ideas/2017-May/045618.html) to have an easier way to write classes in the standard library without the [problems of `namedtuple`s](namedtuples). 13|To that end, *attrs* and its developers were involved in the PEP process, and while we may disagree with some minor decisions that have been made, it's a fine library. 14|If it stops you from abusing `namedtuple`s, it's a huge win. 15| 16|Nevertheless, there are still reasons to prefer *attrs* over Data Classes. 17|Whether they're relevant to *you* depends on your circumstances: 18| 19|- Data Classes are *intentionally* less powerful than *attrs*. 20| There is a long list of features that were sacrificed for the sake of simplicity and while the most obvious ones are validators, converters, [equality customization](custom-comparison), a solution to the [`__init_subclass__` problem](init-subclass), or {doc}`extensibility ` in general – it permeates throughout all APIs. 21| 22| On the other hand, Data Classes do not currently offer any significant features that *attrs* doesn't already have. 23| 24|- We are more likely to commit crimes against nature to make things work that one would expect to work, but that are quite complicated. 25| 26| This includes stepping through generated methods using a debugger, cell rewriting to make bare `super()` calls work, or making {func}`functools.cached_property` work on slotted classes. 27| 28| Our obsession with **developer experience** and quality-of-life features is what *attrs* users report missing most when forced to use Data Classes. 29| 30|- *attrs* doesn't force type annotations on you if you don't like them. 31| 32|- But since it **also** supports typing, it's the best way to embrace type hints *gradually*, too. 33| 34|- While Data Classes implement features from *attrs* every now and then, their presence is dependent on the Python version, not the package version. 35| 36| Handling all these differences is especially painful for PyPI packages that support multiple Python versions. 37| And of course, this includes possible implementation bugs. 38| 39|- *attrs* can and will move faster. 40| We are not bound to any release schedules, and we have a clear deprecation policy. 41| 42| One of the [reasons](https://peps.python.org/pep-0557/#why-not-just-use-attrs) to not vendor *attrs* in the standard library was to not impede *attrs*'s future development. 43| 44|One way to think about *attrs* vs Data Classes is that *attrs* is a **fully-fledged toolkit to write powerful classes** while Data Classes are an easy way to get a class with some attributes – basically what *attrs* was in 2015. 45| 46|But many missing features make Data Classes **not fit for public APIs** beyond pure data containers. 47|For example, unless you build Rube-Goldberg machines around `InitVar`s and custom `__post_init__` methods, you either can't have private field names, or you have to tolerate a public `__init__` method with underscore-prefixed argument names. 48|With *attrs*, you get automatic private field name → public argument name mapping for free – because that's how an idiomatic Python class behaves. 49| 50| 51|## … Pydantic? 52| 53|Pydantic is, first and foremost, a *data validation & type coercion library*. 54|As such, it is a capable complement to class building libraries like *attrs* (or Data Classes!) for parsing and validating untrusted data. 55| 56|However, as convenient as it might be, using it for your business or domain layer [is problematic in several ways](https://threeofwands.com/why-i-use-attrs-instead-of-pydantic/): 57|Is it really necessary to re-validate all your objects while reading them from a trusted database? 58|Should the shape of your web API really apply design pressure on your business objects and therefore business code? 59| 60|In the parlance of [*Form, Command, and Model Validation*](https://verraes.net/2015/02/form-command-model-validation/), Pydantic is the right tool for *Commands*. 61| 62|[*Separation of concerns*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separation_of_concerns) feels tedious at times, but it's one of those things that you get to appreciate once you've shot your own foot often enough and seen the results of allowing design pressure from the edges of your system, like ORMs or web APIs. 63| 64|*attrs* emphatically does **not** try to be a validation library, but a toolkit to write well-behaved classes like you would write yourself. 65|If you'd like a powerful library for structuring, unstructuring, and validating data, have a look at [*cattrs*](https://catt.rs/) which is an official member of the *attrs* family. 66|One of its core tenets is that it doesn't couple your classes to external factors. 67| 68| 69|(namedtuples)= 70|## … namedtuples? 71| 72|{obj}`collections.namedtuple`s are tuples with names, not classes.[^history] 73|Since writing classes is tiresome in Python, every now and then someone discovers all the typing they could save and gets really excited. 74|However, that convenience comes at a price. 75| 76|The most obvious difference between `namedtuple`s and *attrs*-based classes is that the latter are type-sensitive: 77| 78|```{doctest} 79|>>> import attrs 80|>>> C1 = attrs.make_class("C1", ["a"]) 81|>>> C2 = attrs.make_class("C2", ["a"]) 82|>>> i1 = C1(1) 83|>>> i2 = C2(1) 84|>>> i1.a == i2.a 85|True 86|>>> i1 == i2 87|False 88|``` 89| 90|…while a `namedtuple` *intentionally* [behaves like a tuple](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html#tuples-and-sequences), which means the type of a tuple is *ignored*: 91| 92|```{doctest} 93|>>> from collections import namedtuple 94|>>> NT1 = namedtuple("NT1", "a") 95|>>> NT2 = namedtuple("NT2", "b") 96|>>> t1 = NT1(1) 97|>>> t2 = NT2(1) 98|>>> t1 == t2 == (1,) 99|True 100|``` 101| 102|Other often surprising behaviors include: 103| 104|- Since they are a subclass of tuples, `namedtuple`s have a length and are both iterable and indexable. 105| That's not what you'd expect from a class and is likely to shadow subtle typo bugs. 106| 107|- Iterability also implies that it's easy to accidentally unpack a `namedtuple` which leads to hard-to-find bugs.[^iter] 108| 109|- `namedtuple`s have their methods *on your instances* whether you like it or not.[^pollution] 110| 111|- `namedtuple`s are *always* immutable. 112| Not only does that mean that you can't decide for yourself whether your instances should be immutable or not, it also means that if you want to influence your class' initialization (validation? default values?), you have to implement {meth}`__new__() ` which is a particularly hacky and error-prone requirement for a very common problem.[^immutable] 113| 114|- To attach methods to a `namedtuple` you have to subclass it. 115| And if you follow the standard library documentation's recommendation of: 116| 117| ``` 118| class Point(namedtuple('Point', ['x', 'y'])): 119| # ... 120| ``` 121| 122| …you end up with a class that has *two* `Point`s in its {attr}`__mro__ `: `[, , , ]`. 123| 124| That's not only confusing, it also has very practical consequences: 125| for example, if you create documentation that includes class hierarchies like [*Sphinx*'s autodoc](https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/stable/usage/extensions/autodoc.html) with `show-inheritance`. 126| Again: common problem, hacky solution with confusing fallout. 127| 128|All these things make `namedtuple`s a particularly poor choice for public APIs because all your objects are irrevocably tainted. 129|With *attrs* your users won't notice a difference because it creates regular, well-behaved classes. 130| 131|:::{admonition} Summary 132|If you want a *tuple with names*, by all means: go for a `namedtuple`.[^perf] 133|But if you want a class with methods, you're doing yourself a disservice by relying on a pile of hacks that requires you to employ even more hacks as your requirements expand. 134| 135|Other than that, *attrs* also adds nifty features like validators, converters, and (mutable!) default values. 136|::: 137| 138|[^history]: The word is that `namedtuple`s were added to the Python standard library as a way to make tuples in return values more readable. 139| And indeed that is something you see throughout the standard library. 140| 141| Looking at what the makers of `namedtuple`s use it for themselves is a good guideline for deciding on your own use cases. 142| 143|[^pollution]: *attrs* only adds a single attribute: `__attrs_attrs__` for introspection. 144| All helpers are functions in the `attr` package. 145| Since they take the instance as first argument, you can easily attach them to your classes under a name of your own choice. 146| 147|[^iter]: {func}`attrs.astuple` can be used to get that behavior in *attrs* on *explicit demand*. 148| 149|[^immutable]: *attrs* offers *optional* immutability through the `frozen` keyword. 150| 151|[^perf]: Although *attrs* would serve you just as well! 152| Since both employ the same method of writing and compiling Python code for you, the performance penalty is negligible at worst, and in some cases *attrs* is even faster if you use `slots=True` (which is generally a good idea anyway). 153| 154| 155|## … tuples? 156| 157|### Readability 158| 159|What makes more sense while debugging: 160| 161|``` 162|Point(x=1, y=2) 163|``` 164| 165|or: 166| 167|``` 168|(1, 2) 169|``` 170| 171|? 172| 173|Let's add even more ambiguity: 174| 175|``` 176|Customer(id=42, reseller=23, first_name="Jane", last_name="John") 177|``` 178| 179|or: 180| 181|``` 182|(42, 23, "Jane", "John") 183|``` 184| 185|? 186| 187|Why would you want to write `customer[2]` instead of `customer.first_name`? 188| 189|Don't get me started when you add nesting. 190|If you've never run into mysterious tuples you had no idea what the hell they meant while debugging, you're much smarter than yours truly. 191| 192|Using proper classes with names and types makes program code much more readable and [comprehensible](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1304.5257.pdf). 193|Especially when trying to grok a new piece of software or returning to old code after several months. 194| 195| 196|### Extensibility 197| 198|Imagine you have a function that takes or returns a tuple. 199|Especially if you use tuple unpacking (eg. `x, y = get_point()`), adding additional data means that you have to change the invocation of that function *everywhere*. 200| 201|Adding an attribute to a class concerns only those who actually care about that attribute. 202| 203| 204|## … dicts? 205| 206|Dictionaries are not for fixed fields. 207| 208|If you have a dict, it maps something to something else. 209|You should be able to add and remove values. 210| 211|*attrs* lets you be specific about those expectations; a dictionary does not. 212|It gives you a named entity (the class) in your code, which lets you explain in other places whether you take a parameter of that class or return a value of that class. 213| 214|In other words: if your dict has a fixed and known set of keys, it is an object, not a hash. 215|So if you never iterate over the keys of a dict, you should use a proper class. and there's simply more code that can break and thus has to be tested. 222| 223|To bring it into perspective, the equivalent of 224| 225|```{doctest} 226|>>> @attrs.define 227|... class SmartClass: 228|... a = attrs.field() 229|... b = attrs.field() 230|>>> SmartClass(1, 2) 231|SmartClass(a=1, b=2) 232|``` 233| 234|is roughly 235| 236|```{doctest} 237|>>> class ArtisanalClass: 238|... def 246|... if other.__class__ is self.__class__: 247|... return (self.a, self.b) == (other.a, other.b) 248|... else: 249|... return NotImplemented 250|... 251|... def __ne__(self, other): 252|... result = self.__eq__(other) 253|... if result is NotImplemented: 254|... return NotImplemented 255|... else: 256|... return not result 257|... 258|... def __hash__(self): 259|... return hash((self.__class__, or default values. 265|If you pass `order=True`, there's even four more methods: `__lt__`, `__le__`, `__gt__`, and `__ge__`. 266|And who will guarantee you, that you don't accidentally flip the `<` in your tenth implementation of `__gt__`? 267|*attrs* will also do the right thing around [hashing](hashing): 268|It will write a `__hash__` for you if your class should be hashable and marks your class as unhashable if not. 269| 270|Also: no tests whatsoever. 271| 272|It also should be noted that *attrs* is not an all-or-nothing solution. 273|You can freely choose which features you want and disable those that you want more control over: 274| 275|```{doctest} 276|>>> @attrs.define 277|... class SmartClass: 278|... a: int 279|... b: int 280|... 281|... def __repr__(self): 282|... return f"" 283|>>> SmartClass(1, 2) 284| 285|``` 286| 287|:::{admonition} Summary 288|If you don't care and like the sound of your mechanical keyboard, we're not gonna stop you. 289| 290|However it takes a lot of bias and determined rationalization to claim that *attrs* raises the mental burden on a project given how difficult it is to find the important bits in a hand-written class and how annoying it is to ensure you've copy-pasted your code correctly over all your classes. 291| 292|In any case, if you ever get sick of the repetitiveness and the drowning of important code in a sea of boilerplate, you're the author of a third-party library with *attrs* integration, you may want to take advantage of attribute metadata. 141| 142|Here are some tips for effective use of metadata: 143| 144|- Try making your metadata keys and values immutable. 145| This keeps the entire {class}`~attrs.Attribute` instances immutable too. 146| 147|- To avoid metadata key collisions, consider exposing your metadata keys from your modules.: 148| 149| ```python 150| from mylib import MY_METADATA_KEY 151| 152| 153| @define 154| class C: 155| x = field(metadata={MY_METADATA_KEY: 1}) 156| ``` 157| 158| metadata. 161| This is a more graceful approach if your users don't require metadata from other libraries. 162| 163| ```{doctest} 164| >>> from attrs import fields, NOTHING 165| >>> MY_TYPE_METADATA = fields(C).x.metadata[MY_TYPE_METADATA] 184| 185| ``` 186| 187|(transform-fields)= 188| 189|## Automatic Field Transformation and Modification 190| 191|*attrs* allows you to automatically modify or transform the class' fields while the class is being created. 192|You do this by passing a *field_transformer* hook to {func}`~attrs.define` (and friends). 193|Its main purpose is to automatically add converters to attributes based on their type to aid the development of API clients and other typed data loaders. 194| 195|This hook must have the following signature: 196| 197|```{eval-rst} 198|.. function:: your_hook(cls: type, fields: list[attrs.Attribute]) -> list[attrs.Attribute] 199| :noindex: 200|``` 201| 202|- *cls* is your class right *before* it is being converted into an attrs class. 203| This means it does not yet have the `__attrs_attrs__` attribute. 204|- *fields* is a list of all `attrs.Attribute` instances that will later be set to `__attrs_attrs__`. 205| You can modify these attributes any way you want: 206| You can add converters, change types, and even remove attributes completely or create new ones! 207| 208|For example, let's assume that you really don't like floats: 209| 210|```{doctest} 211|>>> def drop_floats(cls, fields): 212|... return [f for f in fields if f.type not in {float, 'float'}] 213|... 214|>>> @frozen(field_transformer=drop_floats) 215|... class Data: 216|... a: int 217|... b: float 218|... c: str 219|... 220|>>> Data(42, "spam") 221|Data(a=42, c='spam') 222|``` 223| 224|A more realistic example would be to automatically convert data that you, for example, load from JSON: 225| 226|```{doctest} 227|>>> from datetime import datetime 228|>>> 229|>>> def auto_convert(cls, fields): 230|... results = [] 231|... for field in fields: 232|... if field.converter is not None: 233|... results.append(field) 234|... continue 235|... if field.type in {datetime, 'datetime'}: 236|... converter = (lambda d: datetime.fromisoformat(d) if isinstance(d, str) else d) 237|... else: 238|... converter = None 239|... results.append(field.evolve(converter=converter)) 240|... return results 241|... 242|>>> {func}`attrs.field()` to define an attribute. 20| 21|They have been added in *attrs* 20.1.0, they are expressive, and they have modern defaults like slots and type annotation awareness switched on by {func}`attr.s` / {func}`attr.ib`, their serious-business aliases `attr.attrs` / `attr.attrib`, and the never-documented, but popular `attr.dataclass` easter egg will stay **forever**. 26| 27|*attrs* will **never** force you to use type annotations. 28| 29| 30|## A Short History Lesson 31| 32|At this point, *attrs* is an old project. 33|It had its first release in April 2015 -- back when most Python code was on Python 2.7 and Python 3.4 was the first Python 3 release that showed promise. 34|*attrs* was always Python 3-first, but [type annotations](https://peps.python.org/pep-0484/) came only into Python 3.5 that was released in September 2015 and were largely ignored until years later. 35| 36|At this time, if you didn't want to implement all the {term}`dunder methods`, the most common way to create a class with some attributes on it was to subclass a {obj}`collections.namedtuple`, or one of the many hacks that allowed you to access dictionary keys using attribute lookup. 37| 38|But *attrs* history goes even a bit further back, to the now-forgotten [*characteristic*](https://github.com/hynek/characteristic) that came out in May 2014 and already used a class decorator, but was overall too unergonomic. 39| 40|In the wake of all of that, [Glyph](https://github.com/glyph) and [Hynek](https://github.com/hynek) came together on IRC and brainstormed how to take the good ideas of *characteristic*, but make them easier to use and read. 41|At this point the plan was not to make *attrs* what it is now -- a flexible class-building kit. 42|All we wanted was an ergonomic little library to succinctly define classes with attributes. 43| 44|Under the impression of the unwieldy `characteristic` name, we went to the other side and decided to make the package name part of the API, and keep the API functions very short. 45|This led to the infamous {func}`attr.s` and {func}`attr.ib` which some found confusing and pronounced it as "attr dot s" or used a singular `@s` as the decorator. 46|But it was really just a way to say `attrs` and `attrib`[^attr]. 47| 48|[^attr]: We considered calling the PyPI package just `attr` too, but the name was already taken by an *ostensibly* inactive [package on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/attr/#history). 49| 50|Some people hated this cutey API from day one, which is why we added aliases for them that we called *serious business*: `@attr.attrs` and `attr.attrib()`. 51|Fans of them usually imported the names and didn't use the package name in the first place. 52|Unfortunately, the `attr` package name started creaking the moment we added `attr.Factory`, since it couldn’t be morphed into something meaningful in any way. 53|A problem that grew worse over time, as more APIs and even modules were added. 54| 55|But overall, *attrs* in this shape was a **huge** success -- especially after Glyph's blog post [*The One Python Library Everyone Needs*](https://glyph.twistedmatrix.com/2016/08/attrs.html) in August 2016 and [*pytest*](https://docs.pytest.org/) adopting it. 56| 57|Being able to just write: 58| 59|``` 60|@attr.s 61|class Point: 62| x = attr.ib() 63| y = attr.ib() 64|``` 65| 66|was a big step for those who wanted to write small, focused classes. 67| 68|### Dataclasses Enter The Arena 69| 70|A big change happened in May 2017 when Hynek sat down with [Guido van Rossum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guido_van_Rossum) and [Eric V. Smith](https://github.com/ericvsmith) at PyCon US 2017. 71| 72|Type annotations for class attributes have [just landed](https://peps.python.org/pep-0526/) in Python 3.6 and Guido felt like it would be a good mechanic to introduce something similar to *attrs* to the Python standard library. 73|The result, of course, was {pep}`557`[^stdlib] which eventually became the `dataclasses` module in Python 3.7. 74| 75|[^stdlib]: The highly readable PEP also explains why *attrs* wasn't just added to the standard library. 76| Don't believe the myths and rumors. 77| 78|*attrs* at this point was lucky to have several people on board who were also very excited about type annotations and helped implement it; including a [Mypy plugin](https://medium.com/@Pilot-EPD-Blog/mypy-and-attrs-e1b0225e9ac6). 79|And so it happened that *attrs* [shipped](https://www.attrs.org/en/17.3.0.post2/changelog.html) the new method of defining classes more than half a year before Python 3.7 -- and thus `dataclasses` -- were released. 80| 81|--- 82| 83|Due to backwards-compatibility concerns, this feature is off by default in the {func}`attr.s` decorator and has to be activated using `@attr.s(auto_attribs=True)`, though. 84|As a little easter egg and to save ourselves some typing, we've also that just set `auto_attribs=True`. 85|It was never documented, but people found it and used it and loved it. 86| 87|Over the next months and years it became clear that type annotations have become the popular way to define classes and their attributes. 88|However, it has also become clear that some people viscerally hate type annotations. 89|We're determined to serve both. 90| 91| 92|### *attrs* TNG 93| 94|Over its existence, *attrs* never stood still. 95|But since we also greatly care about backwards-compatibility and not breaking our users' code, many features and niceties have to be manually activated. 96| 97|That is not only annoying, it also leads to the problem that many of *attrs*'s users don't even know what it can do for them. 98|We've spent years alone explaining that defining attributes using type annotations is in no way unique to {mod}`dataclasses`. 99| 100|Finally we've decided to take the [Go route](https://go.dev/blog/module-compatibility): 101|Instead of fiddling with the old APIs -- whose names felt anachronistic anyway -- we'd define new ones, with better defaults. 102|So in July 2018, we [looked for better names](https://github.com/python-attrs/attrs/issues/408) and came up with {func}`attr.define`, {func}`attr.field`, and friends. 103|Then in January 2019, we [started looking for inconvenient defaults](https://github.com/python-attrs/attrs/issues/487) that we now could fix without any repercussions. 104| 105|These APIs proved to be very popular, so we've finally changed the documentation to them in November of 2021. 106| 107|All of this took way too long, of course. 108|One reason is the COVID-19 pandemic, but also our fear to fumble this historic chance to fix our APIs. 109| 58| 59| 60| 61|## Example 62| 63|*attrs* gives you a class decorator and a way to declaratively define the attributes on that class: 64| 65| 66| 67|```pycon 68|>>> from attrs import asdict, define, make_class, Factory 69| 70|>>> @define 71|... class SomeClass: 72|... a_number: int = 42 73|... list_of_numbers: list[int] = Factory(list) 74|... 75|... def hard_math(self, another_number): 76|... return self.a_number + sum(self.list_of_numbers) * another_number 77| 78| 79|>>> sc = SomeClass(1, [1, 2, 3]) 80|>>> sc 81|SomeClass(a_number=1, list_of_numbers=[1, 2, 3]) 82| 83|>>> sc.hard_math(3) 84|19 85|>>> sc == SomeClass(1, [1, 2, 3]) 86|True 87|>>> sc != SomeClass(2, [3, 2, 1]) 88|True 89| 90|>>> asdict(sc) 91|{'a_number': 1, 'list_of_numbers': [1, 2, 3]} 92| 93|>>> SomeClass() 94|SomeClass(a_number=42, list_of_numbers=[]) 95| 96|>>> C = make_class("C", ["a", "b"]) 97|>>> C("foo", "bar") 98|C(a='foo', b='bar') 99|``` 100| 101|After *declaring* your attributes, *attrs* gives you: 102| 103|- a concise and explicit overview of the class's attributes, 104|- a nice human-readable `__repr__`, 105|- equality-checking methods, 106|- an initializer, 107|- and much more, 108| 109|*without* writing dull boilerplate code again and again and *without* runtime performance penalties. 110| 111|--- 112| 113|This example uses *attrs*'s modern APIs that have been introduced in version 20.1.0, and the *attrs* package import name that has been added in version 21.3.0. 114|The classic APIs (`@attr.s`, `attr.ib`, plus their serious-business aliases) and the `attr` package import name will remain **indefinitely**. 115| 116|Check out [*On The Core API Names*](https://www.attrs.org/en/latest/names.html) for an in-depth explanation! 117| 118| 119|### Hate Type Annotations!? 120| 121|No problem! 122|Types are entirely **optional** with *attrs*. 123|Simply assign `attrs.field()` to the attributes instead of annotating them with types: 124| 125|```python 126|from attrs import define, field 127| 128| 129|@define 130|class SomeClass: 131| a_number = field(default=42) 132| list_of_numbers = field(factory=list) 133|``` 134| 135| 136|## Data Classes 137| packages you use. --- END FILE: README.md --- --- FILE: docs/types.md --- 1|# Type Annotations 2| 3|The addition of static types is one of the most exciting features in the Python ecosystem and helps you write *correct* and *verified self-documenting* code. 4|*attrs* comes with first-class support for type annotations for both {pep}`526` and legacy syntax. 5| 6|However, they will remain *optional* forever, therefore the example from the [README](https://github.com/python-attrs/attrs/blob/main/README.md) could also be written as: 7| 8|```{doctest} 9|>>> from attrs import define, field 10| 11|>>> @define 12|... class SomeClass: 13|... a_number = field(default=42) 14|... list_of_numbers = field(factory=list) 15| 16|>>> sc = SomeClass(1, [1, 2, 3]) 17|>>> sc 18|SomeClass(a_number=1, list_of_numbers=[1, 2, 3]) 19|``` 20| 21|You can choose freely between the approaches, but remember that if you choose to use type annotations, you **must** annotate **all** attributes! 22| 23|:::{caution} 24|If you define a class with a {func}`attrs.field` that **lacks** a type annotation, *attrs* will **ignore** other fields that have a type annotation, but are not defined using {func}`attrs.field`: 25| 26|```{doctest} 27|>>> @define 28|... class SomeClass: 29|... a_number = field(default=42) 30|... another_number: int = 23 31|>>> SomeClass() 32|SomeClass(a_number=42) 33|``` 34|::: 35| 36|Even when going all-in on type annotations, you will need {func}`attrs.field` for some advanced features, though. 37| 38|One of those features is decorator-based functionality like defaults. 39|It's important to remember that *attrs* does not perform any hidden magic here: 40|The decorators are implemented using the object returned by the call to {func}`attrs.field`. 41|Attributes that only carry a class annotation do not have that object, so trying to call a method on it will inevitably fail. 42| 43| 44|## Forward references 45| 46|Python doesn't allow referencing classes in type annotations that haven't been defined yet. 47|Since this is a common requirement in real-world code, the traditional workaround has been defining them using string literals: 48| 49|```python 50|class C: 51| another_c: "C" 52|``` 53| 54|These are called *forward references* ({pep}`526`) and can be enabled automatically for a whole file by using `from __future__ import annotations` ({pep}`563`). 55| 56|As of Python 3.14, this is no longer necessary because it introduced [*deferred evaluation of annotations*](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.14.html#whatsnew314-deferred-annotations) ({pep}`649` and {pep}`749`) that has a more sophisticated system based on {class}`annotationlib.ForwardRef`s, but ultimately solves the same problem. 57| 58|In both cases, if you need to resolve these to real types, you can call {func}`attrs.resolve_types`, which will update the attributes in place. 59| 60| 61|## Class variables and constants 62| 63|Defining an attribute with a type annotation and assigned value looks like a class variable, but it isn't. 64|It's an instance variable with a default value. 65| 66|The correct way to define a class variable is with {data}`typing.ClassVar`, which indicates that the variable should only be assigned in the class (or its subclasses) and not in instances of the class. 67|*attrs* will skip over members annotated with {data}`typing.ClassVar`, allowing you to write a type annotation without turning the member into an attribute. 68|Class variables are often used for constants, though they can also be used for mutable singleton data shared across all instances of the class. 69| 70|``` 71|@attrs.define 72|class PngHeader: 73| SIGNATURE: typing.ClassVar[bytes] = b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n' 74| height: int 75| width: int 76| interlaced: int = 0 77| ... 78|``` 79| 80| 81|## Overview of type checkers 82| 83|Types – regardless how added – are *only metadata* that can be queried from the class and they aren't used for anything out of the box. 84|Some packages like [*cattrs*](https://catt.rs/) or Pydantic use this metadata for runtime type validation and (de-)serialization. 85| 86|But their original purpose is to support static type-checking tools and IDEs. 87| 88|Over the years, the type-checking community has come up with {pep}`681` that defines `dataclass_transform` to offer a baseline way to define dataclass-like class generators. 89|All modern type-checking implementations support that, but in practice it's not enough to make the most out of *attrs*, so some offer further *attrs*-specific support. 90| 91| 92|### Mypy 93| 94|[Mypy] is the original Python type checker and ships with a dedicated *attrs* plugin that implements our features far beyond {pep}`681`. 95| 96|It's the only type checker that supports old-school *attrs* (`@attr.s` / `attr.ib`, including the *type* parameter), but lacks some modern features. 97| 98| 99|### Pyrefly 100| 101|[Pyrefly] is Meta's take on a Rust-based type checker for Python. 102|As of its 1.2 release, it offers significantly more advanced *attrs* support beyond {pep}`681`. 103| 104|Pyrefly only supports modern *attrs* (`@define` / `@frozen` / `field`), but it's also currently the only type checker that supports modern features like {func}`copy.replace`. 105| 106|See their [*attrs* documentation](https://pyrefly.org/en/docs/attrs/) for details. 107| 108| 109|### Pyright / VS Code 110| 111|*attrs* integrates with Microsoft's [Pyright] via {pep}`681`. 112|While Pyright is not as commonly used as a standalone type checker, it's widely used as the foundation of [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/)'s proprietary [Pylance](https://github.com/microsoft/pylance-release) language server that powers [its Python support](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-python.python). 113| 114|Pyright has grown several *attrs*-specific features over the years, but its inferred types are still a tiny subset of those supported by Mypy, including: 115| 116|- Auto-aliasing of private attributes is not
